vtrmc-2003-01.title: Binomial expansion
vtrmc-2003-01.body:
Each day multiplies the money by $\frac65$ (gain) or by $\frac{9}{10}$ (loss), each with probability $\frac12$, independently of the other days.

If there are $p$ gains and $n-p$ losses, the amount is $10000\left(\frac65\right)^p\left(\frac9{10}\right)^{n-p}$, and this happens with probability $\binom np\left(\frac12\right)^n$. Ignoring the insider-trading rule, the expected amount is therefore
$$\sum_{p=0}^n\binom np\left(\frac12\right)^n 10000\left(\frac65\right)^p\left(\frac9{10}\right)^{n-p}=10000\left(\frac12\cdot\frac65+\frac12\cdot\frac9{10}\right)^n=10000\left(\frac{21}{20}\right)^n$$
by the binomial theorem.

The insider-trading rule changes only the outcome $p=n$: its term $\left(\frac12\right)^n10000\left(\frac65\right)^n=10000\left(\frac35\right)^n$ must be replaced by $0$. Hence the average amount after $n$ days is
$$10000\left(\frac{21}{20}\right)^n-10000\left(\frac35\right)^n\ \text{dollars}.$$
**Answer:** $10000\left(\frac{21}{20}\right)^n-10000\left(\frac35\right)^n$ dollars. ∎

vtrmc-2003-01.title: Independence of the daily factors
vtrmc-2003-01.body:
Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be the daily factors; they are independent, each equal to $1.2$ or $0.9$ with probability $\frac12$, so $E[X_i]=1.05$. Without the rule the final amount is $10000X_1\cdots X_n$, whose expectation is $10000\,E[X_1]\cdots E[X_n]=10000\cdot1.05^n$ by independence.

With the rule, the final amount equals $10000X_1\cdots X_n$ except on the event "all gains", which has probability $2^{-n}$ and on which the amount $10000\cdot1.2^n$ is replaced by $0$. So the expectation drops by $2^{-n}\cdot10000\cdot1.2^n=10000\cdot0.6^n$:
$$E=10000\cdot1.05^n-10000\cdot0.6^n.$$
For example, $n=1$ gives $\frac12\cdot0+\frac12\cdot9000=4500=10500-6000$. ∎

vtrmc-2003-02.title: Partial fractions
vtrmc-2003-02.body:
For $|x|<1$ we use the series $-\ln(1-x)=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{x^n}{n}$ (absolutely convergent). Since $\frac1{n(n+1)}=\frac1n-\frac1{n+1}$, and both resulting series converge absolutely,
$$S(x)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{x^n}{n}-\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{x^n}{n+1}.$$
The first sum is $-\ln(1-x)$. For $x\neq0$ the second is
$$\frac1x\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}=\frac1x\left(\sum_{m=1}^\infty\frac{x^m}{m}-x\right)=\frac{-\ln(1-x)-x}{x}.$$
Therefore
$$S(x)=-\ln(1-x)+\frac{\ln(1-x)}{x}+1=1+\frac{1-x}{x}\ln(1-x)\qquad(0<|x|<1),$$
and clearly $S(0)=0$ (which is also the limit of the formula as $x\to0$).

**Answer:** $\displaystyle\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{x^n}{n(n+1)}=1+\frac{1-x}{x}\ln(1-x)$ for $x\ne0$, and $0$ for $x=0$. ∎

vtrmc-2003-02.title: Multiply by $1-x$ (official idea)
vtrmc-2003-02.body:
Multiply $-\ln(1-x)=\sum_{n\ge1}x^n/n$ by $(1-x)$:
$$-(1-x)\ln(1-x)=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{x^n}{n}-\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{x^{n+1}}{n}=x+\sum_{n\ge1}x^{n+1}\left(\frac1{n+1}-\frac1n\right)=x-\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{x^{n+1}}{n(n+1)}.$$
So $\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{x^{n+1}}{n(n+1)}=x+(1-x)\ln(1-x)$, and dividing by $x\ne0$ gives $S(x)=1+\frac{1-x}{x}\ln(1-x)$; $S(0)=0$.

(Check: at $x=\frac12$ the formula gives $1-\ln2\approx0.3069$, and $\frac14+\frac1{24}+\frac1{96}+\frac1{320}+\dots\approx0.3069$.) ∎

vtrmc-2003-03.title: Compare entries
vtrmc-2003-03.body:
The condition says $A$ is symmetric ($A=A'$) and $A^2=I$ ($A=A^{-1}$). Conversely, a symmetric matrix with $A^2=I$ is invertible with $A^{-1}=A=A'$.

Write $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&d\end{pmatrix}$. Then
$$A^2=\begin{pmatrix}a^2+b^2&b(a+d)\\ b(a+d)&b^2+d^2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$

* If $b\neq0$: then $d=-a$ and $a^2+b^2=1$ (the last equation $b^2+d^2=1$ is then the same).
* If $b=0$: then $a^2=d^2=1$, so $a,d\in\{1,-1\}$. This gives $\pm I$ and $\pm\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$; the latter two are of the form $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&-a\end{pmatrix}$ with $a=\pm1$, $b=0$, $a^2+b^2=1$.

So the solutions are exactly
$$A=\pm I\qquad\text{and}\qquad A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ b&-a\end{pmatrix}\ \text{ with } a,b\in\mathbb C,\ a^2+b^2=1,$$
i.e. $b=\pm\sqrt{1-a^2}$ for an arbitrary complex $a$. (Note that over $\mathbb C$, $a$ can be any complex number, e.g. $a=2$, $b=i\sqrt3$.) ∎

vtrmc-2003-03.title: Eigenvalues (official approach)
vtrmc-2003-03.body:
From $A^2=I$, every eigenvalue $\lambda$ satisfies $\lambda^2=1$, so $\lambda=\pm1$ and $\det A=\pm1$.

*Case $\det A=1$.* Then the eigenvalues are equal, both $r=1$ or both $r=-1$, and $A$ is similar to $\begin{pmatrix}r&s\\0&r\end{pmatrix}$ with $s\in\{0,1\}$. Squaring gives $\begin{pmatrix}1&2rs\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=I$, so $s=0$ and $A=rI=\pm I$.

*Case $\det A=-1$.* The eigenvalues are $1,-1$, so $\operatorname{tr}A=0$; with $A$ symmetric, $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&-a\end{pmatrix}$, and $\det A=-a^2-b^2=-1$ gives $a^2+b^2=1$. Conversely such a matrix satisfies $A^2=(a^2+b^2)I=I$ and $A'=A$.

Hence the answer: $\pm I$ and $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&-a\end{pmatrix}$ with $a^2+b^2=1$. ∎

vtrmc-2003-04.title: Seventh roots of unity (official)
vtrmc-2003-04.body:
Let $R=e^{2\pi i/7}$. Since $R\ne1$ and $R^7=1$, $1+R+R^2+\dots+R^6=0$. Taking real parts, $1+\sum_{k=1}^6\cos\frac{2k\pi}7=0$. Using $\cos(2\pi-x)=\cos x$ the sum is $2\left(\cos\frac{2\pi}7+\cos\frac{4\pi}7+\cos\frac{6\pi}7\right)$, and with $\cos(\pi-x)=-\cos x$, $\cos\frac{4\pi}7=-\cos\frac{3\pi}7$, $\cos\frac{6\pi}7=-\cos\frac{\pi}7$:
$$1+2\cos\frac{2\pi}7-2\cos\frac{3\pi}7-2\cos\frac{\pi}7=0.$$
Write $c=\cos\frac\pi7$ and $d=\cos\frac{2\pi}7=2c^2-1$. By sum-to-product, $\cos\frac\pi7+\cos\frac{3\pi}7=2\cos\frac{2\pi}7\cos\frac\pi7=2dc$, so the equation becomes
$$1+2d-4dc=0\iff 4dc-2d=1.$$
With $d=2c^2-1$: $(2c^2-1)(4c-2)=1$, i.e. $8c^3-4c^2-4c+2=1$, so $8c^3-4c^2-4c=-1$ and
$$2c^3-c^2-c=-\frac14.$$
**Answer:** $-\dfrac14$.

vtrmc-2003-04.title: Triple- and quadruple-angle formulas
vtrmc-2003-04.body:
Let $\theta=\frac\pi7$ and $c=\cos\theta$. Since $4\theta=\pi-3\theta$, we have $\cos4\theta=-\cos3\theta$. Now $\cos4\theta=8c^4-8c^2+1$ and $\cos3\theta=4c^3-3c$, so
$$8c^4+4c^3-8c^2-3c+1=0\iff (c+1)(8c^3-4c^2-4c+1)=0$$
(expand to check). As $c\neq-1$, $8c^3-4c^2-4c+1=0$, and dividing by $4$:
$$2c^3-c^2-c=-\frac14.$$
Numerically $c\approx0.9009689$ and $2c^3-c^2-c\approx-0.25000$. **Answer:** $-\frac14$.

vtrmc-2003-05.title: Cyclic quadrilateral $PZXY$
vtrmc-2003-05.body:
As in the diagram, $Q$ and $R$ lie on $BC$, $Z$ lies on segment $PQ$ and $Y$ lies on segment $PR$. Write $\angle A,\angle B,\angle C$ for the angles of triangle $ABC$.

*Step 1: $\angle ZPY=\angle B+\angle C$.* In triangle $PQR$, $\angle PQR=\angle PQC=90^\circ-\angle B$ and $\angle PRQ=\angle PRB=90^\circ-\angle C$. Hence $\angle QPR=180^\circ-(90^\circ-\angle B)-(90^\circ-\angle C)=\angle B+\angle C$, and $\angle ZPY=\angle QPR$.

*Step 2: the medial triangle.* By the midpoint theorem $XY\parallel AB$, $XZ\parallel AC$, $YZ\parallel BC$, so $AZXY$ is a parallelogram and $\angle ZXY=\angle A$; similarly $BXYZ$ is a parallelogram and $\angle ZYX=\angle ZBX=\angle B$.

*Step 3: $P,Z,X,Y$ are concyclic.* In quadrilateral $PZXY$ (convex, with $P$ and $X$ on opposite sides of $ZY$), the opposite angles at $P$ and $X$ add up to $(\angle B+\angle C)+\angle A=180^\circ$. Hence it is cyclic.

*Step 4.* In the circle, the inscribed angles $\angle ZPX$ and $\angle ZYX$ stand on the same chord $ZX$ from the same side, so $\angle QPX=\angle ZPX=\angle ZYX=\angle B$.

*Step 5.* In triangle $PQX$: $\angle PQX=90^\circ-\angle B$ and $\angle QPX=\angle B$, so
$$\angle PXQ=180^\circ-(90^\circ-\angle B)-\angle B=90^\circ.$$
Since $Q,X,C$ are collinear, $\angle PXC=180^\circ-\angle PXQ=90^\circ$. ∎

*Remark.* The facts that $Z\in PQ$ and $Y\in PR$ are read off the diagram; without them the angle conditions alone would not determine $P$.

vtrmc-2003-06.title: Monotonicity
vtrmc-2003-06.body:
*$f$ is injective:* if $f(a)=f(b)$ then $a=f(f(f(a)))=f(f(f(b)))=b$.

*A continuous injective function on an interval is strictly monotone.* (If not, there are $a<b<c$ with $f(b)$ not between $f(a)$ and $f(c)$, say $f(b)>\max(f(a),f(c))$; then any value $v$ with $\max(f(a),f(c))<v<f(b)$ is taken on both $(a,b)$ and $(b,c)$ by the intermediate value theorem, contradicting injectivity. The case $f(b)<\min$ is symmetric.)

*$f$ is not decreasing:* if $f$ were strictly decreasing, then $f\circ f$ would be increasing and $f\circ f\circ f$ decreasing; but $f\circ f\circ f$ is the identity, which is increasing. So $f$ is strictly increasing.

*$f$ is the identity:* suppose $f(x)>x$ for some $x$. Applying the increasing function $f$ repeatedly, $f(f(x))>f(x)$ and $f(f(f(x)))>f(f(x))$, so $x=f^3(x)>f^2(x)>f(x)>x$, a contradiction. Similarly $f(x)<x$ leads to $x<x$. Hence $f(x)=x$ for every $x$. ∎

vtrmc-2003-06.title: Intermediate values (official approach)
vtrmc-2003-06.body:
Suppose $f(y)\neq y$ for some $y$. The three numbers $y,f(y),f^2(y)$ are distinct (if $f^2(y)=y$ then $f(y)=f^3(y)=y$; if $f^2(y)=f(y)$ then applying $f$ gives $y=f^3(y)=f^2(y)=f(y)$). The map $f$ permutes them cyclically: $y\mapsto f(y)\mapsto f^2(y)\mapsto y$.

Among three distinct numbers permuted cyclically, relabel the starting point (replace $y$ by $f(y)$ or $f^2(y)$) and, if needed, $f$ by $g=f^2$ (which is also continuous with $g^3=\mathrm{id}$, and permutes the three numbers in the reverse cyclic order) so that $y<f(y)<f^2(y)$.

Pick $a$ strictly between $f(y)$ and $f^2(y)$. On $[y,f(y)]$, $f$ goes from $f(y)$ to $f^2(y)$, so by the intermediate value theorem $f(p)=a$ for some $p\in(y,f(y))$. On $[f(y),f^2(y)]$, $f$ goes from $f^2(y)$ to $f^3(y)=y<a$, so $f(q)=a$ for some $q\in(f(y),f^2(y))$. Then $p=f^3(p)=f^2(a)=f^3(q)=q$, contradicting $p<f(y)<q$. Hence $f(y)=y$ for all $y$. ∎

vtrmc-2003-07.title: Decompose by the nearest point of $T$
vtrmc-2003-07.body:
Let $U$ be the region. Every point $u\in U\setminus T$ has a unique nearest point $\pi(u)$ in the convex set $T$, at distance $\le1$. Sort the points of $U\setminus T$ by where $\pi(u)$ lies.

**The tetrahedron.** A face is an equilateral triangle of area $\frac{\sqrt3}4$. Its height over a face: the foot of the altitude is the centroid of the face, at distance $\frac1{\sqrt3}$ from a vertex, so the height is $\sqrt{1-\frac13}=\sqrt{\frac23}$. Hence $\operatorname{vol}T=\frac13\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}4\cdot\sqrt{\frac23}=\frac{\sqrt2}{12}$.

**Faces.** Points whose nearest point lies inside a face form the prism of height $1$ standing outward on that face: volume $\frac{\sqrt3}4$ each, $\sqrt3$ for the four faces.

**Edges.** Points whose nearest point lies inside an edge form a wedge of a unit-radius cylinder of length $1$ around the edge, with opening angle $\pi-\delta$, where $\delta$ is the dihedral angle of $T$ (the wedge lies between the two outward normal half-planes of the adjacent faces). Its volume is $\frac{\pi-\delta}{2\pi}\cdot\pi\cdot1^2\cdot1=\frac{\pi-\delta}2$.

To find $\delta$, take edge $BC$ with midpoint $X$ and opposite vertices $A,D$. Then $XA=XD=\frac{\sqrt3}2$, $AD=1$, so by the cosine rule $\cos\delta=\frac{\frac34+\frac34-1}{2\cdot\frac34}=\frac13$. (Equivalently, with $Y$ the foot of the altitude from $D$, $\sin\angle XDY=\frac{XY}{XD}=\frac{1/(2\sqrt3)}{\sqrt3/2}=\frac13$ and $\pi-\delta=\frac\pi2+\sin^{-1}\frac13$.) The six edges contribute
$$6\cdot\frac{\pi-\cos^{-1}(1/3)}2=3\pi-3\cos^{-1}\frac13=\frac{3\pi}2+3\sin^{-1}\frac13.$$

**Vertices.** Points whose nearest point is a vertex $V$ form the intersection of the unit ball at $V$ with the normal cone of $T$ at $V$. The four normal cones at the vertices, translated to a common apex, fill space without overlap (each nonzero direction $w$ is the outward normal at the vertex maximizing $\langle w,\cdot\rangle$, unique for almost every $w$). Hence the four vertex pieces together have the volume of one unit ball, $\frac{4\pi}3$. (Equivalently, as in the official solution: shrinking $T$ to a point keeps this part's volume fixed while the other parts vanish.)

**Total.**
$$\operatorname{vol}U=\frac{\sqrt2}{12}+\sqrt3+\frac{3\pi}2+3\sin^{-1}\frac13+\frac{4\pi}3=\sqrt3+\frac{\sqrt2}{12}+\frac{17\pi}6+3\sin^{-1}\frac13\approx11.77.$$
Equivalent forms: $\sqrt3+\frac{\sqrt2}{12}+\frac{13\pi}3-3\cos^{-1}\frac13$. ∎

vtrmc-2003-07.title: Steiner's formula check
vtrmc-2003-07.body:
For a convex polyhedron $K$, Steiner's formula gives the volume of its $r$-neighbourhood as
$$\operatorname{vol}K+r\cdot\operatorname{area}(\partial K)+r^2\sum_{\text{edges }e}\frac{\ell_e(\pi-\delta_e)}2+\frac{4\pi}3r^3,$$
where $\ell_e$ is the length and $\delta_e$ the dihedral angle at edge $e$. For the regular tetrahedron with edge 1 and $r=1$: $\operatorname{vol}K=\frac{\sqrt2}{12}$, surface area $\sqrt3$, six edges with $\delta=\cos^{-1}\frac13\approx1.23096$:
$$\frac{\sqrt2}{12}+\sqrt3+3\left(\pi-\cos^{-1}\tfrac13\right)+\frac{4\pi}3\approx0.11785+1.73205+5.73189+4.18879=11.77059.$$
This agrees with the first solution (and with a Monte Carlo estimate). ∎
